beats.narration: Good news first: if you packaged the asset, you've already done most of the contribution work. The parameters show it configures. The documented assumptions tell a maintainer what it expects. The bundled eval lets them confirm it still works. Contributing back is moving that asset from private reuse to shared infrastructure — through the channel built for it.

Channel matching first, because it's where most contributions die. The Claude Cookbook is a repository of focused reference implementations — one self-contained pattern, demonstrated end to end. A tool or a fix belongs in that tool's own repository, under its own conventions. And a full multi-component application fits neither. A review process built for one focused pattern can't process an entire app, so the submission stalls unreviewed. Strip the reusable pattern out, and contribute that instead.

wrong channel = stalls unreviewed,

beats.narration: A maintainer accepts what they can verify. The bar is what they need to check, not how clever the code is. Four things clear it: the code does one thing. An example shows it running. A test proves the behavior. And a short statement names the assumptions. Miss one, and the reviewer has to reconstruct your intent — and a contribution that needs reconstruction always goes to the back of the queue.

elements.text: needs reconstruction → back of the queue

beats.narration: Before any technical review comes the gate that decides whether a contribution can be accepted at all: rights and attribution. Code carried out of a customer engagement may be constrained in where it can go. Confirm you have the right to contribute it, and attribute what you built on. When a licensing constraint can't be cleared, don't contribute — escalate to the owner. Skipping this gate is how a merge becomes a problem the legal team has to unwind.

beats.narration: The watch-out is a stalled pull request. Three weeks open, no review. The developer: the code works, I use it every day. The maintainer: it probably works for you — the problem is I can't tell. No test I can run, no example proving the behavior, nothing saying what it assumes. The code was correct. That was never the issue. The author already has all the missing context in their head, which is exactly why the gap is invisible to them. A focused PR with a test and an example gets reviewed fast, because it leaves the maintainer nothing to reverse-engineer.

beats.narration: The reflex: before you open the PR, hand the maintainer the three things they can't reconstruct — the example, the test, the assumptions — and clear the rights gate first. Next, the checkpoint matches three contributions to their channels. Then: requirements and lifecycle.
